history.p: Sometime in the late 1840's Gade asked Hans Christian Andersen to write a text for a new concert piece based on the old Danish ballads "Elveskud" and "Elverhøj", which were very popular at that time. Andersen's text has many features in common with the final version, but for unknown reasons Gade decided not to use it. Neither the printed editions of "Elverskud" nor the concert programmes from Gade's own life time mention the name of the text author, but in 1923 William Behrend revealed that the poet Chr.K.F. Molbech had helped Gade with the text but refused to provide his name for it because Gade kept asking for changes. Then Gade's half cousin, Carl Andersen, took over, making the changes Gade wanted. The editor of the newspaper "Flyveposten", Gottlieb Siesbye, was involved too, but Gade rejected his contribution. The sketches for part one are dated September 1851; however, Gade did not finish the sketches for part three until he had returned from his visit to Leipzig in the spring of 1853. The final score was not ready until March 1854, shortly before the first performance in Musikforeningen on 30 March. "Elverskud" soon became one of Gade's most loved works, not only in Denmark but also abroad. Especially Oluf's Ballade and Morning Song were published in numerous editions and arrangements.

incipText.p: Herr Oluf standsed sin Ganger i Kvæld
Herr Oluf Abends hielt an sein Ross
Nu synker Sol i Luften blaa
In's blaue Meer die Sonne sinkt
Saa tidt jeg rider mig under Ø
So oft mein Auge die Fluren schaut
Læg Sadel paa min raske Hest
Zäum' auf mein Ross mit goldner Kett'
Natten er stille!
Nacht, o wie stille!
Dandsen gaaer saa let gjennem Lunden!
Leicht nun schwebt der Tanz durch die Haine!
Velkommen, Herr Oluf, lad fare din Fig
Willkommen Herr Oluf, was eilst du von hier?
I Øster stiger Solen op
Im Osten geht die Sonne auf
Alt vented jeg ved Borgeled
Ich wartet' an des Hauses Thür
Hør du, Herr Oluf, kjær Sønnen min!
Hör' du, Herr Oluf, sag' an mir gleich
Thi raader jeg hver dannis Svend
Drum rath' ich jedem Jüngling an

physDesc.physMedium: 1 single folio containing sketches for the prologue; 3 bifolios containing sketches for part one, paginated 3-13, last page unnumbered and blank, end-dated "Septemb. / 1851"; 2 bifolios containing sketches for Part Two; 2 bifolios containg sketches for Part Three paginated 1-8, end-dated: "Fine 12. Septr. 1853" and Gade's musical signature; 1 bifolio (fragment) paginated 13-16 written in full score, deleted in red crayon; 1 single folio with a fair copy of the epilogue. Written in ink with many cancellations and emendations in ink and pencil.

Bound in black cloth with leather spine. Written in ink. Paper: 18 staves. Paginated 1-148 in foreign hand. With numerous deletions. German text added in Emil Erslev's hand. End-dated : "Martz 1854" and Gade's musical signature.

annot.p: In a review of the first performance in Copenhagen on 30 March 1854 (Signale für die musikalische Welt, 12/18 (1854), p. 152) the correspondent mentions that the Danish text currently is being translated into German. The German text in Emil Erslev's hand must therefore have been added at a later date.

physDesc.physMedium: Quarter bound with marbled sides and leather spine and corners. On the spine in gold the monogram of King Christian X and: "N.W. GADE / ELVERSKUD / OP. 30 / PARTITUR". Title page stamped "Musikforeningen / København". On verso of title page Gade has written in red ink: "De foretagne Forandringer i Instrumentationen / ere indførte i Partituret 1864. (The changes in instrumentation have been implemented in the score 1864) / Niels W. Gade.". Written in ink. Paper: 16 staves. Paginated from first music page 1-174, followed by pp. 1-7 being the autograph of No. 2 with new instrumentation dated 1864. 2 last pages blank.

annot.p: These parts belongs to a set of parts of which some were printed. As the parts were those that Gade used for many years they include numerous additions and alterations in ink, pencil and red and blue crayon.

physDesc.physMedium: 6 single folios and 1 bifolio. Written in ink by Emil Erslev, Chr. K.F. Molbech and Gottlieb Siesbye with additions by Gade in ink and pencil.
